/**
 * Bytes the app sends to a PTY to wipe the pending input line (the typed-but-
 * unsubmitted text on the prompt). Ctrl+U is the portable choice (#192):
 *
 * - **bash readline**: `unix-line-discard` — kills from the cursor to the start
 *   of the line. With the cursor at end-of-line (the common case when you stop
 *   mid-type and want to abandon what you've typed), that's the whole line.
 * - **claude's TUI input box**: clears the input. Many ink-based TUIs inherit
 *   the readline convention even though their input handling is otherwise
 *   bespoke.
 *
 * Mid-line clear in bash is a known partial: only the left half goes; the user
 * can press Ctrl+K (or Ctrl+E first) to finish the job. We opted for the
 * single, well-known control byte over a multi-byte combo so it works
 * uniformly in both contexts — the Ctrl+A select-all behavior some TUIs use
 * would make a combined Ctrl+A Ctrl+K sequence land the user in a "text
 * highlighted" state in claude.
 */
export const CLEAR_INPUT_BYTES = "\x15";

implementations.vizCode: ({ datatype: 'array', input: [5,3,8,1,9,2,7], run(a) { function siftDown(start, end) { let root = start; for (;;) { const left = 2 * root + 1; if (left > end) return; const right = left + 1; let largest = root; a.cursor('root', root); if (a.compare(largest, left) < 0) largest = left; if (right <= end && a.compare(largest, right) < 0) largest = right; if (largest === root) return; a.swap(root, largest); root = largest; } } const n = a.length; if (n < 2) { a.markSorted(); return; } for (let start = Math.floor(n / 2) - 1; start >= 0; start--) siftDown(start, n - 1); for (let end = n - 1; end >= 1; end--) { a.swap(0, end); a.mark(end, 'sorted'); siftDown(0, end - 1); } a.markSorted(); } })

implementations.code: interface AlgoImpl { id: string; role: string; composes: string[]; } interface KitEdge { from: string; to: string; } interface KitGraph { nodes: AlgoImpl[]; edges: KitEdge[]; } interface NodePos { x: number; y: number } interface KnowledgeLayout { pos: Map<string, NodePos>; world: { w: number; h: number }; bounds: { x: number; y: number; w: number; h: number }; } const NODE_W = 172, NODE_H = 58, COL_PITCH = NODE_W + 208, ROW_PITCH = NODE_H + 22, PAD = 48; function composeDepth(kit: KitGraph): Map<string, number> { const byId = new Map(kit.nodes.map((n) => [n.id, n])); const memo = new Map<string, number>(); const visiting = new Set<string>(); const depth = (id: string): number => { if (memo.has(id)) return memo.get(id)!; const node = byId.get(id); if (!node || node.role === "primitive") { memo.set(id, 0); return 0; } if (visiting.has(id)) return 1; visiting.add(id); const composed = node.composes.filter((c) => byId.has(c)); const d = composed.length ? 1 + Math.max(...composed.map(depth)) : 1; visiting.delete(id); memo.set(id, d); return d; }; for (const n of kit.nodes) depth(n.id); return memo; } export function layoutKitGraph(kit: KitGraph): KnowledgeLayout { const depths = composeDepth(kit); const pos = new Map<string, NodePos>(); const maxDepth = Math.max(0, ...kit.nodes.map((n) => depths.get(n.id) ?? 0)); const rowByCol = new Array<number>(maxDepth + 1).fill(0); for (const n of kit.nodes) { const col = depths.get(n.id) ?? 0; const row = rowByCol[col]++; pos.set(n.id, { x: PAD + col * COL_PITCH, y: PAD + row * ROW_PITCH }); } const maxRows = Math.max(0, ...rowByCol); const cols = maxDepth + 1; const world = { w: PAD * 2 + (cols - 1) * COL_PITCH + NODE_W, h: PAD * 2 + Math.max(maxRows - 1, 0) * ROW_PITCH + NODE_H }; const bounds = { x: PAD, y: PAD, w: world.w - PAD * 2, h: world.h - PAD * 2 }; return { pos, world, bounds }; }

implementations.summary: Sort items by a DECLARED priority ranking of a category — an order deliberately NOT the category's natural/alphabetical one (an attention queue: by urgency, which no property of the state gives you). The ranking is DATA (an array, first = highest), not magic numbers buried in a comparator's ternary chain where the priority cannot be read as a list or reordered without recounting. An UNRANKED category sorts AFTER every ranked one, not to rank 0 — unranked is 'no stated priority', not 'top priority', the trap the `?? 0` hand-version falls into. Stable within a rank; decorate-sort-undecorate so the category is derived once per item, not per comparison. Harvested from the Fleet page's merge queue (#3462/#3465).

// Repo presentation scaffolding (#848 / #1710): turn a planned project into a discoverable repo —
// GitHub topics (from the stack), a thorough README with CI/version badges, and the standard
// community-health files. `handlePublish` applies the output (topics via the Topics API, files via
// the Contents API). This module owns the community-health files and re-exports the README builder
// (`repoReadme.ts`) and the stack matcher (`stackTopics.ts`) so the public surface is one import.

export { deriveTopics, gettingStartedCmds, STACK_TOPICS } from "@/features/planner/lib/stackTopics";
export { buildReadme, type ReadmeFeature, type ReadmeOpts } from "@/features/planner/lib/repoReadme";

export interface ScaffoldFile {
  /** Repo-relative path. */
  path: string;
  content: string;
}

/**
 * The standard community-health files for a new repo. Static, parameterized by the project
 * name. The app commits any that don't already exist (never clobbers a hand-written file).
 */
export function communityFiles(projectName: string): ScaffoldFile[] {
  const name = projectName.trim() || "this project";
  return [
    {

        "Thanks for your interest in contributing!",

        "4. Run the full test suite locally; ensure it passes.",
        "5. Open a pull request targeting `develop` and reference the issue (`Closes #N`).",
        "",
        "## Standards",
        "",
        "- Keep pull requests focused — one concern per branch.",
        "- Write tests for new or changed behavior.",
        "- Follow the existing code style and documentation conventions.",
        "",
      ].join("\n"),
    },
    {
      path: "CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md",
      content: [
        "# Code of Conduct",
        "",
        "## Our Pledge",
        "",
        "We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our",
        "community a harassment-free experience for everyone.",
        "",
        "## Our Standards",
        "",
        "Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment include showing",
        "empathy and kindness, being respectful of differing opinions, and gracefully",
        "accepting constructive feedback. Harassment and other unacceptable behavior will",
        "not be tolerated.",
        "",
        "## Enforcement",
        "",
        "Instances of abusive or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the",
        "project maintainers. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly",
        "and fairly.",
        "",

        "",
      ].join("\n"),
    },
    {
      path: "SECURITY.md",
      content: [
        "# Security Policy",
        "",
        "## Reporting a Vulnerability",
        "",
        "Please do not open a public issue for security vulnerabilities. Instead, report",
        "them privately to the project maintainers (e.g. via a GitHub security advisory).",
        "We will acknowledge your report and work on a fix as quickly as possible.",
        "",
      ].join("\n"),
    },
    {
      path: ".github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md",
      content: [
        "## Summary",
        "",
        "<!-- What does this PR change and why? -->",
        "",
        "Closes #",
        "",
        "## Changes",
        "",
        "-",
        "",
        "## Testing",
        "",

        "- [ ] Tests added/updated for the change",

        "",

bsc-fin--session
implementations.summary: Stored sessions, and the one question the Rust side asks: may an unattended fetch happen right now. The driver NEVER types a credential — a person signs in, the session is stored, everything automated only reuses one. Deliberately NARROWER than the TypeScript policy and conservative against it: it may answer Go only where that one would say use-session.

implementations.name: bsc-fin--inbox
implementations.summary: Where statement exports land, and the rule that stops one being counted twice. Reading the same file again does not error — it doubles a month of spending and every number stays plausible — so a file is CLAIMED once read, moved out of the inbox, and a claim never overwrites. A name whose institution cannot be read is refused rather than guessed, because the wrong profile reads a date as an amount and says so confidently.

implementations.name: bsc-fin--account
implementations.summary: The account registry, and more usefully what it CANNOT tell you. position needs to know what an account IS before a balance means anything, and none of that is in a statement export. Every gap names the capability it silently blocks — an agent's next question after a missing number is always why, and without an answer it invents one. An account NUMBER is refused at any depth.

implementations.name: bsc-fin--txn
implementations.summary: The shared transaction shape, ported from TypeScript. One definition, so the crate does not carry six subtly different ideas of what a transaction is. merchantKey SPLITS FIRST then drops any token carrying a digit — stripping digits first leaves the letter fragments of an order id behind, so one merchant keys differently on every occurrence and matches itself never.

implementations.name: bsc-fin--reconcile
implementations.summary: The gate every derived figure passes through, ported from TypeScript. Arithmetic over an INCOMPLETE transaction list produces a plausible number rather than an error, so reconciliation is a TYPE — and the Rust brand is STRONGER than the TypeScript one: private fields make external construction a compile error with no cast to defeat it.

implementations.name: bsc-fin--position
implementations.summary: What is held and what is owed, as of a date coverage really reaches — the first capability that TAKES a ReconciledLedger. Reads the account REGISTRY directly rather than a parallel declaration type, so bsc fin account feeds it. The sign contract is the whole module: a card statement prints what you OWE, so adding it to a chequing balance produces a quantity that does not exist.

implementations.name: bsc-fin--balance
implementations.summary: Balances, and the conversion that happens at the boundary rather than in somebody's head. A person types what the statement PRINTS — a card says 2431.07 and means you owe it — so the store takes the printed figure and the account's kind and converts. Without the kind the sign is unknowable, so a balance for an undeclared account is refused rather than stored unconverted.
